title: Ὗς καὶ κύων ⟨περὶ εὐτοκίας⟩
titleEn: The Sow and the Dog on Easy Birth
part: The Sow and the Dog on Easy Birth (Chambry 342)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 342. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ὗς καὶ κύων περὶ εὐτοκίας ἤριζον.
sentences.tr: Hys kai kyōn peri eutokias ērizon.
sentences.l: A sow and a dog were contending about bearing well.
sentences.i: A sow and a dog were quarrelling over which of them bore her young the better.
sentences.n: εὐτοκία is bearing offspring easily and well — the good delivery, not the good offspring. The dog is feminine throughout (τῆς κυνός below).

sentences.t: Τῆς δὲ κυνὸς εἰπούσης ὅτι μόνη τῶν τετραπόδων ταχέως ἀποκύει, ἡ ὗς ὑποτυχοῦσα εἶπεν· « Ἀλλ’, ὅταν τοῦτο φράζῃ, γίνωσκε ὅτι τυφλὰ τίκτεις. »
sentences.tr: Tēs de kynos eipousēs hoti monē tōn tetrapodōn tacheōs apokyei, hē hys hypotychousa eipen· « All’, hotan touto phrazēi, ginōske hoti typhla tikteis. »
sentences.l: And the dog having said that she alone of four-footed creatures gives birth quickly, the sow, taking-up-the-word, said: « Well, whenever you say this, know that you bear your young blind. »
sentences.i: When the dog said that she alone among four-footed creatures whelps quickly, the sow took up the word and said: « Whenever you say that, know that what you bear is born blind. »
sentences.n: Another genitive absolute (τῆς κυνὸς εἰπούσης) doing the work an English 'when' clause does. φράζῃ is ambiguous in form — third singular active subjunctive, or second singular middle; the expected second-person active would be φράζῃς, and the sense wants the second person. τυφλά is neuter plural — 'blind things', the puppies.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι οὐκ ἐν τῷ τάχει τὰ πράγματα, ἐν δὲ τῇ τελειότητι κρίνεται.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti ouk en tōi tachei ta pragmata, en de tēi teleiotēti krinetai.
sentences.l: The story shows that things are judged not in speed, but in completeness.
sentences.i: The story shows that things are judged not by how fast they are done but by how finished they are.
sentences.n: One verb, κρίνεται, is held back to the end and serves both limbs, the denied one and the asserted one; ἐν with the dative here is 'by, in respect of'. τελειότης is the state of having been brought to completion.
